### CANDIDATE DETAIL
#### 1. corpus callosum agenesis-abnormal genitalia syndrome  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.790)
**Link type:** shared causal gene (HGNC:18060)

**Proposed mechanism:** ARX (HGNC:18060) —DISRUPTS→ Neuronal development and migration (GO:0048737); Neuronal development and migration (GO:0048737) —LEADS_TO→ Abnormal genitalia (HP:0000018); Neuronal development and migration (GO:0048737) —LEADS_TO→ Dandy-Walker malformation (HP:0011199); Neuronal development and migration (GO:0048737) —LEADS_TO→ Absence of corpus callosum (HP:0001274). Loss-of-function mutations in ARX disrupt normal neuronal development and migration, leading to a spectrum of phenotypes including abnormal genitalia, Dandy-Walker malformation, and absence of the corpus callosum.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of pathogenic variants in ARX that specifically cause one disease phenotype without overlapping with the other, or conversely, identification of distinct causal genes for each disease that do not converge on ARX function. _(variant: Presence of common benign variants in ARX in healthy individuals.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of ARX in these neurodevelopmental disorders could lead to shared therapeutic strategies targeting neuronal development pathways.

**Link type:** shared causal gene (HGNC:18060)

**Proposed mechanism:** ARX (HGNC:18060) —DISRUPTS→ Neuronal development and differentiation (GO:0048666); Neuronal development and differentiation (GO:0048666) —LEADS_TO→ Intellectual disability (HP:0001249); Neuronal development and differentiation (GO:0048666) —LEADS_TO→ Seizures (HP:0001250). Loss-of-function mutations in ARX disrupt normal neuronal development and differentiation, leading to intellectual disability and seizures in both diseases.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of pathogenic variants in ARX that are exclusively associated with one disease but not the other, or variants with gain-of-function effects. _(variant: 0.001)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared mechanism mediated by ARX can inform the development of targeted therapies for both intellectual disability and epileptic encephalopathy, potentially by aiming to restore ARX function or modulate downstream pathways.

**Why it matters:** Understanding the dual role of ARX in neuronal and genital development could inform therapeutic strategies for both conditions, potentially targeting downstream pathways affected by ARX dysfunction.
